questions.q: What is a modern operating system?
questions.a: A resource manager for a computing machine. It controls access to hardware (CPU, I/O, memory) and provides high-level abstractions so application programmers can use the hardware without driving it directly.

questions.q: What are the goals of a modern OS?
questions.a:
1. Efficient resource use: maximise utilisation and avoid bottlenecks.
2. Availability and reliability: systems are critical and data is valuable.
3. User convenience and productivity: user time is expensive.

questions.q: What were batching systems, and what were their advantages and disadvantages?
questions.a:
Early OSes were batch job control systems. Operators had to set up each program's runtime context by hand, so jobs with similar runtime environments were grouped into batches to reduce that work. The OS was a simple control program that worked through the batch one job at a time, with no parallelism.
Problem: I/O is slow and the CPU is fast, so the CPU sat idle during I/O and was under-utilised.
questions.src: Notes W1 'What are Batching Systems?'; S-W1

mcq.q: Why were jobs grouped into batches?
mcq.a: To cut operator work by grouping jobs with similar runtime environments
w: To let several jobs run on the CPU in parallel

To protect the kernel from user programs

mcq.q: What was the main weakness of simple batching systems?
mcq.a: The CPU sat idle while slow I/O completed
w: Too many users shared the machine at once

questions.q: What is pipelined (spooling) batching, and how did it compare with simple batching?
questions.a:
The next step after simple batching. Like CPU instruction pipelining, several jobs run at once but at different stages (e.g. one reading input, one computing, one printing).
Pros: about 30% faster than simple batching.
Cons: still under-utilised, because a slower stage leaves the other stages waiting.

questions.q: What is multiprogramming, and what are its advantages and disadvantages?
questions.a:
Several programs are resident in memory at once, sharing one CPU. When one blocks on I/O, the OS picks another and runs it. While at least one job is ready, the CPU counts as fully utilised. It's the foundation of modern OSes.
It required: job scheduling (which jobs are resident), memory management and protection, and CPU scheduling (fairness between resident jobs).
Pros: very efficient, high hardware utilisation.
Cons: no illusion of parallelism, so it's poor for user interaction.
questions.src: Notes W1 'What is Multi-Programming?'; S-W1

mcq.q: In multiprogramming, when does the OS switch to another program?

mcq.a: No illusion of parallelism, so it's poor for interactive users

mcq.q: Which new OS responsibility did multiprogramming introduce?
mcq.a: Memory management and protection between resident jobs

questions.q: What are time-sharing (multitasking) systems?
questions.a: The natural evolution of multiprogramming. The OS switches between user programs very frequently so many users can interact with the same machine at once. With N users, each effectively gets a computer of 1/N the power. It still switches on I/O blocks too.

mcq.q: What does time-sharing add on top of multiprogramming?

mcq.q: With N users on a time-sharing system, each effectively gets…

w: No CPU time until the others finish

questions.q: What was the personal computer paradigm shift?
questions.a: The final stage of OS evolution: the user is the most important part of the computation, and hardware is cheap. The goal became convenience and responsiveness, not hardware utilisation. Early PCs didn't multitask or support multiple users; these features were added as power grew, and PCs now have multiple processing units in a shared-memory architecture.

questions.q: What are cluster computing and distributed systems?
questions.a:
Cluster: many cheap commodity computers linked by a high-speed LAN, for availability, performance or both.
Distributed system: a loosely coupled collection of processes and clusters that don't share a clock or memory, do share a communication network, are heterogeneous and allow resource sharing.
Issues: load balancing, process migration, distributed transactions, security, communications and reliability.

questions.q: What is a process, and why is it the most fundamental concept in an OS?
questions.a:
A process is a program in execution: an abstraction of a running program, a container holding everything needed to run it, and an entity with an address space and a set of resources. It has text (code), data and stack segments, plus open files, the PC, registers and stack pointer.
It's the most fundamental concept because every program runs as one or more processes.

questions.q: When does a process run kernel code, and how does it get there?
questions.a: A process normally runs in user mode. When it needs a service the OS provides, it makes a system call, which traps into the kernel and switches to kernel mode. The modes give different privilege levels; separating them protects the OS from errant users.

questions.q: What are the five process states?
questions.a:
New: being created.
Ready: waiting to run on the CPU.
Running: its instructions are executing.
Blocked (waiting): waiting for I/O or an event.
Terminated: finished.
The scheduler moves Ready → Running; a timer interrupt moves Running → Ready; an I/O request moves Running → Blocked; I/O completion moves Blocked → Ready.

questions.q: What fields does a PCB hold, and where is it stored?
questions.a:
Process ID (unique number), program counter (next instruction), registers (stack pointer, index registers…), scheduling info (priority, pointer to scheduling queue), memory structure (page/segment tables, base register), open file table, and accounting info (CPU time, page faults, time limits…), plus the process state. Exact contents depend on the system.
PCBs live in kernel space, not user space, for protection. The OS keeps a process table: one PCB entry per process.

questions.q: How does the OS regain control of the CPU from a running process?
questions.a:
While a process runs, the dispatcher isn't running, so the OS has lost control. It gets it back through:
Traps (internal, software): a system call, an error (illegal instruction, addressing violation, divide by 0) or a page fault.
Interrupts (external, hardware): a key typed, a disk operation completing, or the hardware timer at the end of a time slice.

questions.q: What is the difference between preemptive and cooperative multitasking?
questions.a:
Preemptive: the OS can interrupt a running process (e.g. on a timer) and give the CPU to another.
Cooperative: a running process must voluntarily give up the CPU before another can run, so one misbehaving process can hog the CPU.

questions.q: What is the difference between independent and cooperating processes, and why use cooperating processes?
questions.a:
Independent processes can't affect or be affected by other processes. Cooperating processes can, and they communicate using IPC.
Advantages of cooperating:
• Information sharing: concurrent access to shared files and resources
• Speedup: while one is blocked on I/O, another computes
• Modularity: smaller programs doing specific tasks is safer, better design
• Convenience: users want to do several things at once

questions.q: What is RPC, and how does it relate to the two IPC variants?
questions.a: IPC lets cooperating processes communicate, through shared memory (fast and convenient, but needs synchronisation) or message passing (no conflicts, easy, good for small data). RPC (remote procedure call) is a type of IPC that runs a procedure in another address space over a network, as if it were a local call.

questions.q: What happens when a process forks, and how does a process terminate?
questions.a:
Fork: the parent creates a child, then either keeps running alongside it or waits for it to terminate. The child gets a different PID and runs the same program from the same PC (or a different program after exec).
Three steps: (1) allocate and initialise a new process structure, including a PCB; (2) duplicate the parent's whole context, including virtual memory; (3) schedule the child to run. The parent is blocked while the child is created.
Termination: voluntarily with exit, or involuntarily from a signal (e.g. kill). A status code is returned to the parent, and a waiting parent then resumes.

questions.q: What are the key benefits of using threads?
questions.a:
Efficiency: creating and switching threads is cheaper than processes.
Sharing: threads share memory and files, so no expensive IPC.
Responsiveness: another thread can run when one blocks (a same-process switch may be cheaper, but isn't free).
Multiprocessing: threads of one process can run on different cores at once. On one core threads take turns (concurrency); on many cores they run together (parallelism).

questions.q: Compare user threads and kernel threads.
questions.a:
User threads: managed entirely in user space by a library (e.g. pthreads); cheap and fast; the kernel is generally unaware of them, so they can't exploit full multiprogramming/multiprocessing.
Kernel threads: managed by the kernel (TCB / thread table in the kernel); expensive and slow to create; support true multiprogramming and multiprocessing; exist to support user threads.

questions.q: Describe the thread models for mapping user threads onto kernel threads.
questions.a:
Many-to-one: many user threads on one kernel thread. Low cost; supports multiprogramming but not multiprocessing (threads of one process can't run in parallel).
One-to-one: each user thread gets a kernel thread. Expensive, but supports multiprogramming and multiprocessing.
Many-to-many: M user threads on N kernel threads (M > N). Neither too slow nor blocking, but difficult to program.
Hybrid: many-to-one + one-to-one.

questions.q: What is concurrency, and why can it be a problem?
questions.a: Concurrency is the simultaneous execution of threads and processes: actual simultaneity on multiple cores/processors, or apparent simultaneity through time slicing. Concurrent threads usually access shared data; if that sharing is uncontrolled, the data can become inconsistent or incorrect. The fix is synchronisation.

questions.q: What are the three requirements for a critical-section solution?
questions.a:
Mutual exclusion: only one thread in the critical section at a time.
Progress: if the critical section is free and a thread wants to enter, only threads in their entry/exit sections may take part in deciding who enters (and the decision can't be postponed forever).
Bounded waiting: there's a finite bound on how many times a waiting thread must stand aside for others.

questions.q: What is Peterson's solution, and what are its problems?

• Limited to two threads/processes (variations exist for more)
• Busy waiting: a waiting thread keeps checking flag and turn in a loop, wasting CPU time

questions.q: What are atomic machine instructions, and what are their problems?
questions.a:
Hardware assistance: special CPU instructions that execute atomically.
Test-and-Set: sets the lock to true and returns its original value.
Swap: exchanges two values.
They guarantee mutual exclusion and progress, but not bounded waiting, since they can't arbitrate who goes next.
Problems: busy waiting, and starvation (e.g. a frequently scheduled high-priority process keeps grabbing the lock while a low-priority one rarely gets it).

questions.q: What problem do sleep/wakeup primitives solve, and how do mutex locks and condition variables work together?
questions.a:
They avoid busy waiting.
Sleep/wait: blocks the process so it doesn't burn CPU while it waits.
Wakeup/signal: unblocks a waiting process so it can try again.
Mutex + condition variable: the mutex is a boolean saying whether the lock is free. If the condition isn't met, the thread waits on the CV, which releases the lock and sleeps; when the condition becomes true, another thread signals to wake a waiter. Acquiring the mutex itself may still involve a short busy wait.

questions.q: What is the producer-consumer problem, and how can a count variable with sleep/wakeup solve it?
questions.a:
Producers and consumers share a common buffer: producers insert items, consumers remove them. Uncontrolled access causes race conditions.
Count-based solution: keep a count of items.
• Buffer full → producer sleeps
• Buffer empty → consumer sleeps
• Buffer no longer full → wake the producer
• Buffer no longer empty → wake the consumer
count is itself shared, so access to it must be protected; the course then solves this properly with semaphores.

questions.q: What is the difference between counting and binary semaphores?
questions.a:
A semaphore is an integer signalling mechanism with atomic P() (down/acquire/test) and V() (up/release/increment).
Counting semaphore: any value from 0 up. Controls a resource with n instances: initialise to n; the first n threads decrement it to 0; later threads wait.
Binary semaphore: only 0 (locked) or 1 (unlocked). Used for mutual exclusion with a P(mutex)…V(mutex) pair. Test-and-Set can make P and V atomic.

questions.q: How do you solve the producer-consumer problem with semaphores?
questions.a:
Use three semaphores: mutex = 1 (mutual exclusion on the buffer), empty = N (free slots), full = 0 (filled slots).
Producer: P(empty); P(mutex); insert; V(mutex); V(full).
Consumer: P(full); P(mutex); remove; V(mutex); V(empty).
Order matters: doing P(mutex) before P(empty)/P(full) can deadlock (a thread sleeps while holding the mutex).

Deadlock: processes wait on each other's semaphores in a cycle.

questions.q: What are monitors, and how do they differ from semaphores?
questions.a:
A higher-level synchronisation construct that bundles shared data and the operations on it into one structure. Only one thread can execute a monitor's methods at a time, so mutual exclusion is automatic, rather than the programmer placing every wait()/signal() by hand as with semaphores. Condition variables are still used inside the monitor for waiting and signalling.
CV vs semaphore: semaphores count resources (an integer); CVs wait for a condition to become true.

questions.q: What is deadlock, and what is the Dining Philosophers problem?
questions.a:
Deadlock: a set of processes is deadlocked if each is waiting for an event that only another process in the set can cause, so none can proceed. It happens because resources are finite.
Dining Philosophers: n philosophers sit at a round table, alternating between thinking and eating. There's one chopstick between each pair (n in total), and eating needs both neighbouring chopsticks. If every philosopher picks up their left chopstick at once, everyone waits for the right one forever: deadlock. It illustrates resource sharing, deadlock and starvation.

questions.q: What is a resource allocation graph, and what does a cycle tell you?
questions.a:
A visual model of resource assignment, used to formalise deadlock. It contains a set of processes (circles) and resources (boxes, with dots for instances). A request edge goes P → R; an assignment edge goes R → P.
No cycle → no deadlock. With single-instance resources, a cycle means deadlock; with multiple instances, a cycle means deadlock is possible but not certain.

questions.q: What are the four strategies for handling deadlock?
questions.a:
1. Ignore it (the "ostrich" approach): do nothing; most general-purpose OSes do this.
2. Detect and recover: allow deadlocks, detect them, then fix them.
3. Dynamic avoidance: check each request before granting it, keeping the system in a safe state.
4. Prevention: break one of the four necessary conditions.

questions.q: How can each deadlock condition be broken to prevent deadlock?
questions.a:
Mutual exclusion: generally not possible to eliminate.
No preemption: if we wait on a resource held by another waiting process, preempt it and give it to us. Not always possible.
Hold and wait: release everything held before waiting, or request all resources at once. Poor utilisation; popular resources can cause starvation.
Circular wait: impose an ordering on resource requests; multiple resources of the same type must be requested together.
Prevention in general can lower device utilisation and throughput.
questions.src: Notes W6 'How does preventing deadlock work for each condition?'; S-W6

questions.q: How do deadlock avoidance and deadlock detection/recovery work?
questions.a:
Avoidance: a state is safe if there's a sequence in which every process can finish; all other states are unsafe. The OS only grants requests that keep the state safe. It needs prior knowledge of each process's maximum needs. Unsafe doesn't always mean deadlock, but safe guarantees none. Costs: lower utilisation and overhead from the safety check.
Detection: if we don't prevent or avoid, check current allocations against availability to find deadlocked processes.
Recovery: preemption, rollback to a checkpoint, or killing processes.

questions.q: Define the CPU scheduling criteria.
questions.a:
CPU utilisation: keep the CPU as busy as possible (used/available).
Throughput: number of threads that complete per time unit.
Response time: time from submitting a request until the first response.
Waiting time: time spent waiting in the ready queue.
Turnaround time: time from submission to finish.

questions.q: What are the scheduling goals for each category of system?
questions.a:
All systems: fairness (fair share of CPU), balance (keep the system busy), policy enforcement.
Multiprogramming (batch): throughput, turnaround time, CPU utilisation.
Interactive: response time, proportionality (meet user expectations).
Real-time: meet deadlines, predictability (e.g. audio/video).

questions.q: What is the difference between CPU-bound and I/O-bound processes, and why does it matter?
questions.a: Processes alternate between CPU bursts and periods waiting for I/O. A CPU-bound process has long CPU bursts and little I/O; an I/O-bound process has short CPU bursts and frequent I/O waits. The CPU burst distribution affects the choice of scheduling algorithm (e.g. favour I/O-bound jobs to keep devices busy and interactive programs responsive).

questions.q: Compare FIFO, SJF and SRTF scheduling.
questions.a:
FIFO: simple, non-preemptive; short jobs get stuck behind long ones.
SJF: run the process with the shortest next CPU burst. Optimal: minimum average waiting time. But the OS can't know the next burst length, so it has to estimate it, and long jobs can starve (unfair).
Non-preemptive SJF lets the current process finish its burst. Preemptive SJF = SRTF (shortest remaining time first): if a new arrival's burst is shorter than the current process's remaining time, preempt.

w: It has too many context switches

questions.q: How does round-robin scheduling work, and what is the longest a thread waits?
questions.a:
Each thread gets a quantum q of CPU time. When it expires, the thread is preempted and put back on the ready queue. With n threads, each gets 1/n of the CPU, and no thread waits more than q(n−1) for its next quantum.
q large → behaves like FIFO, less responsive. q small → more responsive but more context-switch overhead, so q must be much larger than a context switch.
Pros: good response time. Cons: context-switch overhead.

mcq.a: It is preempted and returned to the ready queue
w: It moves to the blocked state
It keeps running until it does I/O

mcq.q: What is the main cost of round robin?
w: Needing to know burst lengths in advance

questions.q: What is priority scheduling, what problem does it have, and how is it fixed?
questions.a:
Each process gets an integer priority, and the CPU goes to the highest priority. Non-preemptive: a newly arrived higher-priority task waits for the current task to release the CPU. Preemptive: it takes the CPU immediately.
Problem: starvation; low-priority processes may never run.
Fix: ageing; a process's priority rises the longer it waits.

mcq.a: It raises a process's priority the longer it waits

questions.q: How do multilevel queues and multilevel feedback queues differ?
questions.a:
Multilevel queue: the ready queue is split into fixed queues, e.g. foreground (interactive, RR) and background (batch, FIFO). There's fixed priority between queues (foreground first), so background jobs can starve.
Multilevel feedback queue: processes can move between queues as their behaviour changes, which also implements ageing. It's defined by: the number of queues and their algorithms, plus methods to choose a process's initial queue, upgrade it and demote it.

questions.q: What are dynamic loading and dynamic linking?
questions.a:
Both reduce memory consumption.
Dynamic loading: load a routine into memory only when it's called; the rest stays on disk.
Dynamic linking: instead of copying library code into every program, shared libraries are linked at run time (a stub locates the library), so many programs share one copy.
Note: your notes say "at compile time". It's run time; compile-time copying is static linking.

questions.q: What is address binding, and when can it happen?
questions.a:
Binding maps program addresses to memory: symbolic (e.g. count) → relocatable ("14 bytes from the start of this module", by the compiler) → absolute (e.g. 74014, by the linker/loader).
Compile time (embedded systems): the compiler produces absolute addresses.
Load time (early OSes): the loader turns relocatable addresses into absolute ones; if the base changes, reload.
Execution time (modern OSes): hardware maps logical to physical addresses at run time, so a process can be moved while running. This enables compaction and dynamic loading.

questions.q: What is the difference between logical and physical addresses, and what does the MMU do?
questions.a:
Logical (virtual) address: generated by the CPU at run time, from the process's point of view; it doesn't exist physically. The logical address space is all logical addresses a program generates.
Physical address: a real location in RAM. The physical address space is the matching set of physical addresses.
The MMU is hardware that maps virtual to physical addresses at run time; user programs never see real physical addresses.
Relocation-register scheme: the relocation (base) register holds the smallest physical address; the limit register holds the range of logical addresses. physical = logical + relocation, if logical < limit; otherwise trap. Each process can only reach its own space.

questions.q: What is contiguous allocation, and how do fixed and variable partitions compare?
questions.a:
Memory is split into two partitions: the OS (usually low memory, with the interrupt vector) and user processes (high memory). Each process sits in a single contiguous block.
Fixed partitions: memory is statically divided into partitions of set sizes; a process gets the smallest free partition that fits. Fast with per-size free lists, but inflexible and wasteful (internal fragmentation).
Variable partitions: sized to each process's needs, but leave holes of various sizes scattered through memory (external fragmentation). Holes are chosen with first fit (first hole big enough) or best fit (smallest hole big enough, leaving the smallest leftover).

questions.q: What is the difference between internal and external fragmentation, and how is external fragmentation reduced?
questions.a:
Internal fragmentation: allocated memory is slightly larger than requested; the unused space is inside a partition.
External fragmentation: enough total free memory exists, but it isn't contiguous.
Compaction reduces external fragmentation by shuffling memory contents so all free memory forms one large block. It needs execution-time binding, and can't be done while I/O is in progress on the memory being moved.

questions.q: How does segmentation work, and what fragmentation does it suffer?
questions.a:
Non-contiguous allocation splits a program into small units placed anywhere in memory (needs hardware support): segmentation, paging, or paged segmentation.
Segmentation: the program is a collection of logical segments (main program, function, stack…). A segment table in memory maps the 2D logical address (segment, offset) to a 1D physical address. Each entry has a base (starting physical address) and a limit (segment length).
Each segment is contiguous in physical memory, but segments needn't be next to each other.
Internal fragmentation: generally no; each segment gets exactly what it needs.
External fragmentation: yes; free memory breaks into holes between segments.

questions.q: How does paging work, and what fragmentation does it suffer?
questions.a:
Divide logical memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into frames of the same size. To run an n-page program, find n free frames (the OS keeps a free-frame list) and load it. A page table per process (stored in its context) maps each page number → frame number.
Internal fragmentation: yes; the last page may not be full.
External fragmentation: no; any free frame can hold any page, even if scattered.
Note: your notes say "maps page to page". It maps page → frame.

mcq.q: Why does paging avoid external fragmentation?
mcq.a: Any free frame can hold any page, so pages needn't be contiguous

questions.q: How does paged segmentation combine segmentation and paging?
questions.a: Partition the program into segments, then partition each segment into pages. Each segment has its own page table; the segment-table entry points to that segment's page table (and holds its length). A logical address is (segment, page, offset): the segment number selects the page table, the page number selects the frame, and the offset is added. This keeps segmentation's logical view while avoiding its external fragmentation.
kw: each segment has a page table
